name: アジアンダイニング 金魚蘭 (Asian Dining Kingyoran)

claims.text: No information available about cross-contamination controls. The kitchen fries karaage and spring rolls; a shared fryer is likely but unconfirmed.
No gluten-free soy sauce (tamari) is mentioned anywhere. Standard wheat-containing shoyu is almost certainly used in marinades and sauces across the menu.
Fish sauce and oyster sauce are standard condiments in Thai and Vietnamese cooking; the kitchen does not label or disclose their use on any documented menu or listing.
TripAdvisor reviewers note staff are friendly and accommodating despite no English menu, but no allergy protocol or allergen sheet is documented on any platform.
A vegetable pho (五目フォー) is a standing menu item, suggesting some plant-forward dishes exist alongside meat-heavy ones.

Every item in the shop is made with wheat flour. There is no gluten-free preparation area or gluten-free product line. Cross-contamination with wheat is a certainty throughout the kitchen and counter.
No soy sauce is listed as an ingredient in any bread or bagel product; the primary allergen across all items is wheat flour itself.

Bagels are baked alongside dairy-containing varieties in the same oven. Plain and some unflavoured bagels may share trays with cheese or butter bagels. No dedicated vegan production line is indicated.

No published allergy protocol or staff allergy-training information was found. Each product does carry an allergen label on the website, which is the only formal allergen disclosure available. Visitors with serious allergies should ask staff to point to the relevant label.
Most plain natural-yeast bagels list only wheat in their allergen declaration — no eggs or dairy — making them one of the clearer egg-free and dairy-free options in Himeji for non-celiac visitors.

name: 播州姫路本町たまごや (Banshu Himeji Honmachi Tamagoya)

claims.text: Not a dedicated gluten-free facility; kitchen cross-contamination risk is unconfirmed. No allergen separation policy is published.
The house original soy sauce (tare) is a custom wheat-brewed shoyu co-developed with a local manufacturer. It is not gluten-free. Coeliacs should bring their own tamari or GF soy sauce.
One FindMeGlutenFree reviewer specifically advises bringing your own soy sauce to this restaurant.
Bonito flakes (katsuo-bushi) are sprinkled on rice by default; must be requested omitted. Miso soup dashi type is unconfirmed but likely katsuobushi-based given regional Harima red-miso tradition.

Reviewers on FindMeGlutenFree describe staff as helpful and accommodating when dietary needs are communicated clearly. One celiac diner reported eating rice, eggs, and pickled plums safely after asking about ingredients.
The core ingredients — farm-fresh raw egg over plain white rice — are naturally wheat-free and suitable as a baseline for gluten-avoiders who communicate clearly with staff.

name: ビストロ料理とワインのお店 NicolaS (Bistro Ryori to Wine no Mise NicolaS (Nicola)

claims.text: No information on cross-contamination protocols is documented in any source. The kitchen is run solo by one chef in a compact basement space, and house-made bread is prepared on-site, raising surface/utensil contamination concerns for celiac diners.

No source mentions wheat-free soy sauce or any soy sauce substitution. French-Italian bistro cooking typically uses wheat-containing sauces, pasta, and bread — no gluten-free accommodations are documented.
Animal products (butter, cream, lard, stock, cured meats) are core to every menu category; vegan cross-contact risk is high and no plant-only prep area or labeling is mentioned.
No reviewer or source mentions allergy awareness, allergen menus, or staff training. Diners with serious allergies should phone ahead (079-244-9082) and discuss needs directly with the chef.

The restaurant is run by a single owner-chef who cooks to order in a small kitchen — this one-cook format means custom requests can be discussed directly with the decision-maker, rather than relying on front-of-house staff to relay information.

name: cafe&izakaya ふぁぶｰる (Cafe & Izakaya Faveur)

claims.text: The kitchen prepares breaded katsu, meunière (wheat-flour coated), karaage, and pizza — all high-gluten preparations. No information on fryer separation or allergen protocols has been published anywhere.
Standard wheat-containing soy sauce is almost certainly used in marinades and seasoning throughout the menu; no tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned on any platform.
The entire menu is built on meat and seafood with no plant-based dishes; animal-derived ingredients including dashi, meat stocks, and dairy (Basque cheesecake) are core to the cooking.

No allergen menu, allergy-handling policy, or staff dietary-accommodation language appears on Tabelog, HotPepper, Gurunavi, or Hitosara. Diners with serious allergies should call ahead: 050-8885-9357.
The entire menu is wheat-centric — bread, pastries, burgers, and sandwiches are the core offering. No allergen labelling or cross-contamination management information was found on any source.
Bread spread includes butter and egg-based items; American-style sweets contain dairy. No dairy-free or vegan cross-contact protocols mentioned.

name: クラフトジンとおでん専門店 maruya (Craft Gin to Oden Senmonten Maruya)

claims.text: The shared oden pot simmers all ingredients together; no separate preparation for allergen-free orders is mentioned.
Oden is served with ginger soy sauce (shoga joyu), which is standard wheat-containing shoyu and a direct gluten source. No tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned.
Dashi broth is made with Rausu kombu, bonito flakes, and tuna flakes. All oden items, including vegetables, are cooked in this fish-based broth — unavoidable cross-contact for vegans.
Oden is a simmered dish with no deep-frying involved, eliminating fryer cross-contamination as a concern.

name: ネパールインド料理 ダルバル (DARBAR (Nepal India Ryori Darubaru))

claims.text: Naan is baked in a clay tandoor that is also used for wheat-flour breads; airborne wheat flour in the kitchen is a realistic concern for celiac diners. No information on separate prep areas was found.
Soy sauce is not used in Nepalese or Indian curry cooking. No soy sauce wheat risk identified for curry dishes here.

Ghee (clarified butter) is commonly used in Indian restaurant cooking and may appear in curry bases or applied to naan; no source confirms it is absent from the vegetable curries. Ask the kitchen directly.
No allergy menu, allergen chart, or staff allergy-handling protocol was found on any source. Direct inquiry in Japanese is necessary before ordering.

Indian and Nepalese curry bases are naturally free of Japanese soy sauce (shoyu), dashi, mirin, and other common Japanese hidden-wheat or hidden-fish ingredients. Rice is available with all set menus as a wheat-free starch alternative to naan.
